introduction-compliance-by-design.core: Privacy engineering builds data protection into systems rather than bolting it on (GDPR Article 25: data protection by design and by default). It starts with data minimisation, collecting only what's needed, then applies technical controls matched to the use: tokenisation and encryption for operational systems, pseudonymisation for internal analytics, and anonymisation techniques (k-anonymity, differential privacy) for sharing or publishing. The goal is useful data with provably limited risk to individuals.

first_principles.problem: An analytics team receives full production customer tables 'just in case', and a laptop theft becomes a reportable breach.
truths: Data you don't hold can't leak.

analogy.title: Designing a house with frosted bathroom windows from the start
analogy.story: Privacy is part of the blueprint, not curtains added after the neighbours complain.
analogy.breaks: Windows are fixed; data flows change with each new feature, so privacy reviews must recur.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each data flow gets proportionate protection.

code.text:
| Use                       | Technique                    |
|---------------------------|------------------------------|
| Payments service          | Tokenisation (vault)         |
| Internal BI dashboards    | Pseudonymised IDs + RBAC     |
| Sharing with researchers  | k-anonymity / generalisation |
| Publishing statistics     | Differential privacy         |

check.q: What's the most effective privacy control?
check.a: Data minimisation: not collecting or keeping data you don't need.

data-minimization-and-the-right-to-be-fo.core: Data minimisation means collecting, processing and retaining only the personal data needed for a stated purpose. The right to erasure (GDPR Art. 17) means deleting a person's data on request across every system: primary DBs, replicas, caches, search indices, analytics, logs and backups. That's only feasible if you know where the data lives (a data map), key it consistently by subject ID, enforce retention TTLs, and use techniques like crypto-shredding for immutable stores and backups.

first_principles.problem: A deletion request removes a user from Postgres, but their data lives on in Elasticsearch, S3 exports, Kafka topics and three years of backups.
derivation: Maintain a **data map** by subject ID.

analogy.title: Shredding a document means finding every photocopy
analogy.story: If copies were made and filed everywhere, shredding the original isn't enough.
mapping: Burning the key to a locked box
analogy.breaks: Photocopies are physical; digital copies multiply silently through pipelines.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Erasure covers immutable copies without editing backups.

code.text:
# each user's PII is encrypted with their own data key
ct = encrypt(kms_data_key(user_id), pii)
# erasure: destroy the key; every copy (backups, Kafka, S3) becomes unreadable
key_store.delete(user_id)
audit.log("erasure", user_id, systems=["pg", "es", "s3", "kafka", "backups"])

check.q: How does crypto-shredding handle data in backups?
check.a: Destroying the per-user encryption key makes all encrypted copies, including backups, unreadable.

pseudonymization-vs-anonymization-a-lega.core: Pseudonymisation replaces direct identifiers with tokens or hashes, but the data can still be linked back to a person using additional information (a key or lookup table), so it is still personal data under GDPR, though it reduces risk. Anonymisation means individuals can no longer be identified by any reasonably likely means, and only then does GDPR stop applying. Hashing emails is not anonymisation: hashes can be reversed by dictionary attack, and the remaining attributes can re-identify people.

first_principles.problem: A company shares 'anonymised' data with SHA-256 hashed emails, and a partner re-identifies users by hashing its own customer list.
truths: Hashes of known values are reversible by guessing.
derivation: Use **keyed HMAC/tokens**, with keys held separately.

analogy.title: Removing name tags at a party versus making guests truly unrecognisable
analogy.story: Without name tags, friends still recognise faces; true anonymity needs masks, height changes and voice changers.
analogy.breaks: Disguises are visible; re-identification risk in data is invisible without analysis.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Partners can't reverse tokens, but GDPR still applies.

code.text:
import hashlib, hmac
hashlib.sha256(b"alice@example.com").hexdigest()     # anyone can recompute → linkable
hmac.new(SECRET_KEY, b"alice@example.com", "sha256").hexdigest()
# keyed: not recomputable without the key, but still pseudonymous (key holder can link)

check.q: Why is a SHA-256 hash of an email not anonymous?
check.a: Anyone with a list of emails can hash them and match, re-identifying people.

k-anonymity-hiding-in-the-crowd.core: Most people can be uniquely identified by a few quasi-identifiers: ZIP code, birth date and sex identify about 87% of Americans (Sweeney). k-anonymity requires that every record be indistinguishable from at least k−1 others on its quasi-identifiers, achieved by generalisation (exact age to 30–39, ZIP 02139 to 021**) and suppression (removing outliers). An attacker who knows someone's quasi-identifiers can then narrow them down only to a group of k.

first_principles.problem: A hospital releases visit records without names, and a journalist identifies the governor's record from his ZIP, birth date and sex.

analogy.title: Hiding in a crowd wearing the same uniform
analogy.story: If at least five people look identical, a witness can't say which one you are.
analogy.breaks: If everyone in the crowd shares the same secret, hiding among them doesn't protect the secret.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Linking by ZIP + age + sex now finds three candidates, not one.

code.text:
Before:  ZIP 02139, age 34, F, flu
         ZIP 02138, age 36, F, asthma
         ZIP 02141, age 31, F, diabetes
After:   ZIP 021**, age 30-39, F, {flu | asthma | diabetes}
         → each person hides among 3 identical-looking rows

check.q: What is an equivalence class in k-anonymity?
check.a: A group of records sharing identical quasi-identifier values, which must contain at least k records.

the-failure-of-k-anonymity-homogeneity-a.core: k-anonymity hides who you are within a group but not what the group reveals. In a homogeneity attack, all k records in a group share the same sensitive value (everyone has cancer), so membership reveals it. In a background knowledge attack, an attacker rules out values. Linkage across multiple releases or auxiliary datasets (as in the Netflix Prize de-anonymisation) can shrink groups. l-diversity and t-closeness patch some gaps, but these syntactic methods lack formal guarantees, which motivates differential privacy.

first_principles.problem: A 5-anonymous dataset still reveals a neighbour's HIV status, because all five records in her group are HIV-positive.
derivation: Account for **auxiliary data** and repeated releases.

analogy.title: A crowd where everyone wears the same badge saying 'Patient, Oncology Ward'
analogy.story: You can't tell which person is your neighbour, but you know she's an oncology patient.
analogy.breaks: Real crowds change; static datasets can be cross-referenced forever.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Leaky groups are found before release.

code.text:
qi = ["zip3", "age_band", "sex"]
g = df.groupby(qi)["diagnosis"].nunique()
print(g[g < 2])   # groups where every record has the same diagnosis
# any row printed = membership reveals the diagnosis (l-diversity < 2)

check.a: Each equivalence class must contain at least l well-represented distinct sensitive values.

differential-privacy-the-gold-standard.core: Differential privacy (DP) is a mathematical guarantee: the output of an analysis is almost equally likely whether or not any single individual's data is included, so nothing specific about one person can be learned, regardless of the attacker's auxiliary knowledge. It works by adding calibrated random noise (Laplace or Gaussian) scaled to the query's sensitivity divided by ε (epsilon). Smaller ε means more privacy and more noise. A privacy budget limits cumulative ε across queries. It's used by the US Census, Apple and Google.

first_principles.problem: A company wants to publish usage statistics, but repeated, precise queries could reveal individual users' behaviour.

analogy.title: Asking a survey question where each person flips a coin to decide whether to answer truthfully
analogy.story: Overall percentages are still accurate, but no single answer can be trusted to reveal that person (randomised response).
analogy.breaks: Coin flips are simple; real DP calibrates noise mathematically to each query's sensitivity.

check.q: What happens to privacy as more DP queries are answered on the same data?
check.a: Privacy loss adds up (composition), so a total budget must cap the number or precision of queries.

tokenization-protecting-data-at-rest.core: Tokenisation replaces a sensitive value (card number, SSN, email) with a non-sensitive surrogate token that has no mathematical relationship to it. The mapping lives only in a secured token vault, or is derived with format-preserving encryption in vaultless designs. Downstream systems store and process tokens, keeping real data out of most of the stack and out of compliance scope. Only a few authorised services can detokenise. Tokens can preserve format (last four digits) for usability.

first_principles.problem: SSNs stored in 40 tables across 12 services mean every one is a breach risk and in audit scope.
truths: Tokens have no exploitable relationship to data.

analogy.title: A cloakroom ticket
analogy.story: You hand over your valuable coat and get a numbered ticket that's worthless to a thief; only the cloakroom can swap it back.
analogy.breaks: Cloakroom tickets are random; vaultless tokenisation uses keyed encryption, so key security matters.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Most systems handle only tokens; the real values stay in one place.

code.text:
vault write transform/encode/payments value=4111-1111-1111-1111 transformation=card
# encoded_value: 5732-8810-4471-1111   (format kept, last 4 preserved)
vault write transform/decode/payments value=5732-8810-4471-1111 transformation=card
# only the payments service's policy allows decode

check.q: How does tokenisation differ from encryption for scope reduction?
check.a: Systems holding tokens have no key or mathematical way to recover data, so they can be out of scope; encrypted data with accessible keys usually isn't.
